## 2. Did we actually need a Social Network 'sequel'?

**Score:** 178
**Body:** What are people’s thoughts on *The Social Network* getting a sequel?

On one hand, it makes sense. Social media, tech billionaires, misinformation, politics, AI, and the way these platforms shape real life have only become more relevant since the first movie.

But I’m curious peoples thoughts:

Did David Fincher need to come back? Did it come out too late? Even if you haven't seen it I am curios your thoughts. I am still thinking about it especially with the first one being an all time fav.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Just got out of it. I don't see it as a sequel. Companion piece is definitely an appropriate explanation to the film. It's hard to live up to the original, but I still really enjoyed this one
2. What if the real sequel was the friends we made along the way
  - Zuck lost all his friends along the way
    - It's called "winning".
  - The friends we had inside all along... 
3. Yes. Because the first one was the story of Facebook. 

This will be the story of Meta. 

Both are evil. but for different reasons. 


4. I think it’s sad that people still support scum like Zuckerberg, Gates, Musk, and Bezos. 

Not because they are billionaires, but because they are POS billionaires who do nothing to better America or communities like they could. They’re manipulative, selfish, and greedy with bad intentions. 
5. I will never understand this "need" nonsense. We always need a good movie. If it is, great if not. Move on 

  
Same with the even dumber "who asked for this" as if anyone asked for most of the great movies today.

  

6. I kinda think we did.

The first movie came out during a time when general public opinion of Zuck was pretty high.  It was kind of a risk, at the time, to be taking shots at him, but in hindsight the film was right on the money.

This one seems less about Zuck and Facebook themselves than about social media corporations trying to censor their critics while allowing dangerous behavior and even encouraging it through their algorithms.  It asks the question “should the people who host the forum be allowed to control what people say on it?”

IE I don’t actually think they’re comparable movies other than both of them involving Mark Zuckerberg and Facebook.
7. Need? No. 

But we also have never needed a movie in the entire history of film, because there's no such thing as needing a movie, only wanting them.

## 3. Mouse Hunt is an exceptionaly well crafted family film that should be considered among the best in its genre.

**Score:** 152
**Body:** It's DNA lies in Home Alone, The Witches, Adams Family and pretty much every comedic double act going back to Laurel and Hardy, but i sincerly believe that Mouse Hunt is one of the last films before the millennium that fully encapsulates the magic of physical, family comedy and presents it in almost perfect form.

The chemistry between the brothers is ludicrously fun and, as a brother myself, i would say also oddly relateable. The plot has them navigate the complexities of sharing the responsibilities of their late father's estate and its really well developed, sincerely handeled and doesn't really sugar coat it much for the kids either. The characters are going through the motions emotionally and you feel that.

The set pieces are as timeless as anything else in its genre that came before it, while being fresh enough to still hold up today. If you like that kind of surreal high energy comedy of course, and I think its a shame we didn't see Nathan Lane and Lee Evans do something together again, i think they made a quite hilarious double act that could quite early of carried over into a series of other movie ideas.

I love that there is only one (I think) proper FX shot in the whole film and they used 65 trained live mice, all of whom where unharmed throughout the entire of production. Personally I approve of trained mice in the workplace, and this effort absolutely made the film, as much as the real actors themselves did. Its important to note that at this time, they absolutely could have made the mouse using FX for large parts of the film, lots of movies were starting to use it, but they chose not to and it pays off 30 years later, no doubt.

The jazzy score from Alan Silvestri is fantastic, especially partnered with that over stylised cartoonish/gothic production on set. Its such an off-kilter, fun and surreal film to watch these days. I can't recall the last time a film remotely like it came out.

If I had buried a 90s time capsule, Mouse Hunt would be in there, wedged somewhere between Muppet Treasure Island and Babe in the wholesome, Sunday afternoon hooters department.

### Top 8 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Nathan Lane is a national treasure. 
  - 100% Agree. 

As a Brit, despite him being very clearly American. I always found his delivery and comedic style has quite a bit British quirk to it.

He has a great voice. Reminds me of some of our eccentric radio play stars of the 60s and 70s. He'd have suited Carry On.

3. Christopher Walken's best role?

I have a theory that he thought he was on the set of Ghostbusters and that he assumed Nathan Lane was Dan Aykroyd. But I'll save that for another time...

But yeah, iconic.

5. This is Gore Verbinski’s directorial debut. Excellent movie!

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. I think Digger made me depressed...

**Score:** 62
**Body:** Saw this movie a week ago and still haven't really snapped out of this heavy melancholy it gave me once the credits stopped.

Dwelling on it for a week I've come to realize that the most lasting impact the film had on me was after the meta "Level 4" announcement during the credits where the music was replaced with nature sounds: birds, bugs, bullfrogs. 

I've read somewhere that part of those nature sounds were bird calls of endangered UK bird species which of course adds to the poignancy.

But when hearing it I realized: I don't think there was a live animal or plant anywhere in the movie... 

We had the animatronic cat of course, and Digger's sprawling, misty estate was just miniatures made of plastic.  Even the ocean water towards the end of the play was a plastic mylar sheet. 

It's all plastic and fake, and this movie shows us the bleak "Do Androids Dream-esque" future where animals are replaced with automatons because they're all already extinct.

And it really, *really* bums me out. Because it's really happening. We are losing the bugs and the birds and natural habitat and someday within our lifespans it really will all turn to wet, semi-submerged, cold concrete where the air is poison and artificial intelligence polices us.

And at that point, the birds and bugs and bullfrogs will sound like music.

## 3. Italian Permissiveness

**Score:** 31
**Body:** Lately while perusing the list of the "Video Nasties" that caused moral hysteria in Britain in the 1980s, something occurred to me that I had never considered before.

A great number of them were produced in Italy. On reflection, that shouldn't have surprised me. I've seen plenty of ultraviolent Italian horror films from the likes of Lucio Fulci and his contemporaries. There are also "shocking" films among the canon of highbrow Italian cinema. *Saló* most obviously, but equally other Pasolini films or the like of *Satyricon* etc. 

But, it wasn't until I saw so many Italian titles accumlated together in one place that it occurred to me that, "*that's pretty fucking odd, isn't it?*". 

Why was late 20th century, Catholic Italy the place that gave filmmakers free reign to gouge out eyeballs, disembowel and cannibalise? 

Why was this, seemingly, so much less controversial in Italy than in the comparably secular UK? Are Catholics more liberal towards the arts than Protestants? That would make a certain amoung of sense when you consider the history of gruesome Catholic paintings of hell.

However, I myself come from a similarly Catholic western European nation and the likes of *Zombie Flesh Eaters* or *Cannibal Holocaust* could never have been made here. Still to this day nothing even vaguely comparable has been produced. 

On thinking about it a little further it occurred to me that Italy also had a flourishing porn industry in this period. Even if my theory about Catholics being tolerant towards art has some basis in truth surely the same would not be extended to pornography? Like the extreme horror, my own country has never had a porn industry of any consequence. 

So what is the answer? Why was late 20th century Italy such a sanctuary for the production of extreme horror and pornography?

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The answer isn't simple. I'll try my best for a concise response. 
There are a wide variety of commercial and cultural influences at play here. 

First, the commercial. The Italian film industry had been linked to American and British cinema almost since its inception. It fell into a post-WWI crisis that nearly destroyed it entirely. This created an environment in which artistic risk was not commercially viable. Thus, the few films that *were* produced were modeled off the films making money, i.e. American films.

During the fascist era, Mussolini made this a specific policy. He figured that to create a great, national cinema, he should model the Italian film industry off the most successful film industry there is: Hollywood. This didn't change just because fascism fell and Neorealism took over. In fact, Neorealist films were often failures in Italy and survived because of international markets where they received the most acclaim. To capture the domestic market, most Italian films were still comedies, melodramas, and swashbucklers.

Given this, with the rise of Hollywood historical epics like *Quo Vadis*, *Helen of Troy*, and *Ben Hur*, Italian filmmakers naturally tried their hand at the genre. 

(Edit: the Hollywood on the Tiber phenomenon, in which American/British companies cut costs by filming their large scale epics at the newly rebuilt Cinecitta Studios in Rome, is worth mentioning here.)

The one-two punch of *Attila* and *Hercules* (both distributed stateside by Joseph E. Levine) finally opened the American market to Italian genre cinema. Such *peplum*/sword and sandal films became the preeminent commercial force in Italian cinema as a result. This created something called the "genre cycle," in which Italian producers would pump out as many similarly styled films as possible within the few years a given trend was popular. When *peplum* fell out of favor, for instance, spaghetti Westerns and Eurospy took up the mantle.

Italian horror evolved similarly. Riccardo Freda and Mario Bava had worked for years to crack the international market by styling their horror films after the Hammer horror trend coming out of Britain. Bava finally succeeded with *Black Sunday*, which opened the flood gates for bloody *giallo* films a few years later. Though *gialli* are deeply rooted in Italian style and pop culture, the success of *Psycho* certainly enabled their rise. Thus, the Italian slasher was born and survived into the modern slasher period of the late 70s/80s.

It is worth noting here that like Neorealism, Italian horror was generally *not* successful in Italy and was made with international markets in mind. Thus, they continued to look internationally for inspiration. The flood of Italian zombie films, for instance, came following the international success of *Dawn of the Dead* (an Italo-American co-production, but American all the same). Extreme slasher films followed the success of *Halloween*. Cannibal films were initially modeled off of, of all movies, *A Man Called Horse*. Italian filmmakers were very inventive and creative with their construction and influences, but projects were ultimately greenlit to fall in line with what was popular.

Culturally, the 1960s were a great time of boundary breaking experimentation across the world. This includes boundaries of censorship. The Hayes Code in Hollywood cinema was formally abolished in the 1960s, and ideas of sexual expression were becoming more mainstream. There was an appetite and a willingness to allow greater freedom in artistic expression. This extended to Italy as well. Legislation like prison reforms and labor protections began to pass under organized pressure from the left. Artistic license naturally followed.

This isn't to say such reforms were universally accepted. In Italy in particular, socio-political tensions regarding the limits of progress and the fears of fascism came to a head in 1968 with the beginning of the Years of Lead. This was a multi-decade period of domestic terrorism that was essentially a low-level civil war. The entire country was in a fearful and depressive malaise that naturally extended to its arts and entertainment. Italian filmmakers went so extreme with their exploitation cinema because 1. it was a calling card that was different from its peers, making them stand out for sheer novelty alone, and 2. there was a lot of everyday misanthropic violence that fueled such forms of commercial expression.

International sentiment factored in as well. West Germany, one of the most reliable markets for Italian exploitation, was dealing with their own domestic terror issues with the Red Army Faction. The United States was reeling from the national embarrassment of the Vietnam War and the Watergate scandal. Successive oil crises destroyed Western economies. It was a very low period all around.

At the same time, leftist movements like second-wave feminism were found threatening to the (particularly male) establishment. Extreme sexual violence in Italian exploitation was itself a conservative reaction to women's liberation. Things like nazisploitation and the racial dynamics of cannibal films were similarly reactionary to a depressed society dealing with an existential identity crisis.

Eventually, censorship under the guise of moral integrity *did* begin to creep up in the early 1980s. The infamous seizure of *Cannibal Holocaust* was rooted in this growing campaign to reel in extreme cinema. Several additional factors worked in tandem to destroy the Italian exploitation industry, including the shutdown of grindhouses (itself rooted in complex societal responses to the AIDS and crack epidemics), the rise of home video, and the general crisis that affected Italian cinema in the 1980s.

## 4. Say Anything (1989) - surprisingly good

**Score:** 9
**Body:** I knew with Cusack in the lead and Cameron Crowe writing & directing this would be decent but I was surprised just how good it was.  
  
I thought it would be more along the lines of The Sure Thing (1985) which was solid, but not a classic like Rob Reiner’s other fodder from his golden early period, with the iconic boom-box scene most likely making for a goofy romantic gesture at the end.  
  
Nope. It appears mid-film and is quite a serious moment. In fact the film is much more of a serious drama than I expected. Way more authentic, like Richard Linklater’s Before Trilogy. It still has a rich vein of comedy, but that’s just a side dish to a raw and complex look at youth, love and values.  
  
The big surprise was John Mahoney as Diane’s boomer dad - a rich and layered character with a journey you don’t see coming.  
  
Every time a high school comedy cliche looked like it was about to come around the corner the film batted it away and did something far more interesting and honest instead. These are real, intelligent characters navigating complex emotional challenges.  
  
The film delivered a wallop I wasn’t expecting, and makes the likes of Superbad seem like dumb slop for kids (as much as I enjoy that film 🤫)

## 5. The Descent (2005) and Neil Marshall's career

**Score:** 9
**Body:** I was rewatching *The Descent* recently. I have nothing new to say about it, really; it's an objectively terrific horror movie and an incredibly well-made, well-written movie overall. Any criticisms you could level at it come from the fact that it's such a well-oiled script for horror that it sometimes seems like the next beat could be predicted (unless you go in totally blind, which would be an amazing experience).

But the layers of conflict in the story are something worth studying if you ever wanted to write a film -- there's the character-based stuff, like Juno's affair with the dead husband our protagonist still grieves for (resolved within the context of the horror plot very well), the environmental/production design horror of just having characters enter a caving system, get lost, and the impending sense of doom via claustrophobia. Those two things is technically enough for a good horror movie but to add a third layer, the creatures, means the viewer is constantly engaging with the plot in a much more complex manner than you'd expect for a "horror movie where a large group of characters get plucked off violently one-by-one" style thing.

So Marshall writes, directs and releases *The Descent* to very earned praised and success, and it's earned a legacy 20 years later as a truly great film of the 00s from what I've seen -- eg lists of best horror films, best films from the UK etc in the media. 

But Marshall, given 7 (!) moderately or well-funded opportunities to direct a script he writes, drops the ball every single time subsequently (imo). No original concept he's written or directed since has hit anywhere close to the sense of mastery in *The Descent* (or even *Dog Soldiers,* his debut), which is so strange because I feel like *The Descent* acts as the ultimate proof that it's writer and director has real juice. Even if you subjectively didn't like it, it objectively 'works' as a story and film in a way that everything else he makes does not. 

Is this just a guy that had 1-2 amazing ideas up his sleeve and nothing else? Is this something to do with the way the UK film industry works?  Am I completely wrongheaded here and *The Descent* is good because (say) it had a very hands on producer or editor who guided some of Marshall's poorer instincts we'd see in later films? It almost makes me think of DePalma on a smaller scale, wherein DePalma spent decades making even the most ludicrous concepts fun and gripping but then all of a sudden post *Mission Impossible* he literally lost the ability to put good video on screen -- not a fair analogy, very different legacy and obviously DePalma was like 70 by the 2000s, but still.
